title: Node
body:
Data plus a [[Pointer]] to the next one. The whole idea of a [[Linked Structure]] is in those
two fields.

```c++
struct Node {
	int   data;
	Node* next;
};
```

**A struct cannot contain itself, but it can contain a pointer to itself.** `Node next;` is a
[[Compile Errors|compile error]] (the compiler would need infinite space to lay it out);
`Node* next;` is 4 or 8 bytes and is fine. That one line is what makes linked lists possible,
and it is the fact worth memorising out of this whole section.

Nodes are allocated one at a time with [[new And delete|new]], so they live on the heap and
the structure grows to fit the data instead of being sized in advance like an [[Array]]. See
[[Dynamic Allocation]] and [[Stack and Heap]].

```c++
Node* p = new Node;
p->data = 7;
p->next = NULL;      // the last node's next is always NULL
```

`p->data` is shorthand for `(*p).data`: dereference, then take the field. You will write the
arrow far more often than the dot.

Two invariants to keep in your head, because every list bug is one of them:

- The last node's `next` is `NULL`. That is how you know when to stop walking.
- `head` names the first node, or is `NULL` for an empty list. Lose `head` and the whole list
  is unreachable, which is also a memory leak.

Nodes are not only for lists. A node with two pointers instead of one is a [[Tree]]; a node
with several is a [[Graph]]. [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] takes it from here and asks what each
arrangement costs.
